name: Secant root iteration
variables: f scalar residual; x_k current estimate; x_(k−1) previous estimate
assumptions: Two distinct starting points near a simple root and nonzero divided differences
limitations: No bracket is preserved and near-equal residuals destabilize the update
failure_conditions: No bracket is preserved and near-equal residuals destabilize the update
computation: One new function evaluation per step after initialization

source.citation: NIST DLMF §3.8(iii), Eq. 3.8.6 and Secant Method. https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.8.E6

application: Invert a monotone calibration map when derivative evaluation is unavailable

name: Halley root iteration
variables: f scalar residual; f′ and f″ its derivatives; x_k current estimate
assumptions: Smooth f, simple root, nearby initialization and nonzero denominator
limitations: A small denominator or poor initialization can produce an arbitrarily large step
failure_conditions: A small denominator or poor initialization can produce an arbitrarily large step
computation: One evaluation each of f, f′ and f″ per step
application: Invert a smooth fitted quantile equation when both derivatives are cheap
required_inputs: A scalar equation or fixed-point map from a timestamped prior fit, or an explicitly defined synthetic function.

name: Steffensen fixed-point acceleration
definition: u=g(x_k), v=g(u), x_(k+1)=x_k−(u−x_k)²/(v−2u+x_k). Return x_k if u=x_k.
variables: g scalar fixed-point map; u and v successive images of x_k
assumptions: Locally smooth map, fixed point with g′≠1 and nonzero second difference away from convergence
limitations: Cancellation can dominate the denominator near a fixed point; a safeguard is needed when it vanishes
failure_conditions: Cancellation can dominate the denominator near a fixed point; a safeguard is needed when it vanishes
computation: Two evaluations of g per accelerated step
application: Accelerate convergence of an iterated one-dimensional shrinkage equation
required_inputs: A scalar equation or fixed-point map from a timestamped prior fit, or an explicitly defined synthetic function.
